title: Form Follows Function: Bridging Neuroscience and Architecture

findings.antecedent: Unwanted noise (below hearing loss levels)
findings.consequent: Immune, cardiovascular, endocrine, sleep, emotional, cognitive responses
findings.mechanism: Noise acts as an environmental stressor disturbing various physiological and cognitive functions.
findings.quote: unwanted noise, at intensity levels below those known to cause noise-induced hearing loss, may disturb immune, cardiovascular, endocrine, sleep, emotional, and cognitive responses [6].

findings.antecedent: Low, unwanted, competing, or disturbing sound levels
findings.mechanism: Competing sounds interfere with cognitive processing and ability to rest.
findings.quote: Even low sound levels, if unwanted, competing or disturbing, may be associated with diminished speech intelligibility, lowered cognition, and lack of rest, along with increased stress responses [7].

findings.antecedent: Low, unwanted, competing, or disturbing sound levels
findings.mechanism: Unwanted sounds contribute to increased physiological and psychological stress.
findings.quote: along with increased stress responses [7].

findings.antecedent: Daytime noise levels > 65 dB(A)
findings.mechanism: High noise levels act as a chronic stressor, impacting cardiovascular health.
findings.quote: The Environmental Expert Council found a consistent trend toward an increased cardiovascular risk if the daytime noise levels exceed 65 dB(A) [8].

findings.antecedent: Long-term low-frequency traffic noise exposure (avg < 55 dB(A))
findings.mechanism: Chronic noise exposure, even at low levels, can disrupt the endocrine system and lead to stress.
findings.quote: Chronic stress reactions, such as cortisol disturbances, have been observed in children with long-term low-frequency traffic noise exposure averaged at less than 55 dB(A) [9].

findings.antecedent: Emergency and intensive care units
findings.quote: Edelstein et al. (2008) logged continuous sound levels in emergency and intensive care units and found average levels ranging from 75 to 85 Leq dB(A)

findings.antecedent: Intensive care units
findings.quote: Averaged sound pressure levels in intensive care units were up to 10 times greater than conversational speech.

findings.antecedent: Healthcare environments (past 50 years)
findings.quote: healthcare environments have been steadily increasing over the past 50 years, with no single facility operating within the sound levels recommended by the World Health Organization [11].

findings.antecedent: Ambient noises
findings.mechanism: Competing auditory stimuli interfere with the detection and interpretation of target sounds.
findings.quote: ambient noises mask the perception of body sounds [12].

findings.antecedent: Competing sounds or noise (wanted or unwanted)
findings.consequent: Perception and attention to speech and sound signals
findings.mechanism: Distracting auditory stimuli reduce the ability to perceive and attend to relevant speech and sound signals.
findings.quote: competing sounds or noise, wanted or unwanted, mask perception and attention to speech and sound signals [13].

findings.antecedent: Noisy environments (flight or ambulances)
findings.mechanism: Environmental noise interferes with the auditory information required for accurate diagnosis.
findings.quote: diagnostic accuracy by means of stethoscope auscultation is diminished in flight or ambulances [14].

findings.antecedent: Elevated sound levels (competing alarms, equipment, conversations, mechanical systems)
findings.mechanism: Competing sounds reduce the clarity and comprehension of spoken words.
findings.quote: elevated sound levels from competing alarms, equipment, conversations, and mechanical systems may interfere with speech intelligibility

findings.antecedent: Elevated sound levels (competing alarms, equipment, conversations, mechanical systems)
findings.mechanism: Auditory confusion caused by noise contributes to errors in identifying similar-sounding medications.
findings.quote: and be a factor in “look-alike-sound-alike” medication errors [15].

findings.antecedent: Knowing location (vs. being lost) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: The cognitive state of knowing one's location versus being lost is reflected in distinct patterns of brain activity.
findings.quote: reveal differences in brain dynamics when subjects know their location compared with EEG components when they are lost.

findings.antecedent: Spaces rich with visual cues (vs. ambiguous spaces devoid of cues) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: The presence and absence of visual information in an environment differentially activate brain regions involved in spatial processing.
findings.quote: Differences in EEG responses associated with spaces rich with visual cues versus ambiguous spaces devoid of cues were found in parietal and occipitotemporal cortex.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with less visuospatial information (disorientation) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: Increased cognitive load and attentional demands in disorienting environments lead to stronger theta synchronization.
findings.quote: A significantly stronger synchronization in theta waves and stronger desynchronization in the lower alpha band of EEG frequencies was observed.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with less visuospatial information (disorientation) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: Increased cognitive load and attentional demands in disorienting environments lead to stronger alpha desynchronization.
findings.quote: A significantly stronger synchronization in theta waves and stronger desynchronization in the lower alpha band of EEG frequencies was observed.

findings.antecedent: Disorientation in spaces with less visuospatial information in VR environment
findings.mechanism: Increased attentional demands to navigate in ambiguous spaces are reflected in alpha wave desynchronization.
findings.quote: Disorientation in spaces with less visuospatial information was associated with increased alpha wave desynchronization, likely reflecting increased attentional demands [20].

findings.antecedent: Absence of obvious visual cues (in ambiguous VR space)
findings.consequent: Search for distinguishing features (shadows, patterned finishes)
findings.mechanism: Humans actively seek out environmental information for wayfinding when explicit cues are not provided.
findings.quote: In the case where obvious cue were not presented, subjects looked for any distinguishing features that might indicate location, including shadows around doors, or patterned finishes.

findings.antecedent: Ineffective wayfinding design (in one hospital)
findings.consequent: Staff time spent giving directions to lost patients
findings.mechanism: Poor spatial design leads to increased operational burden and costs.
findings.quote: McCarthy (2004) reported that in one hospital, 4,500 h each year were spent by staff giving directions to lost patients, with an associated cost equivalent of $220,000 per annum [21].

findings.antecedent: Ineffective wayfinding design (compromising clean/contaminated space separation)
findings.consequent: Severe consequences, potentially fatal (during infectious epidemics)
findings.mechanism: Poor spatial organization can lead to breaches in infection control, posing significant health risks.
findings.quote: the consequence of ineffective wayfinding design may have more severe consequences, and may even prove fatal during infectious epidemics, should the separation between clean and contaminated spaces be compromised.

findings.antecedent: Diurnal light/dark cycle
findings.mechanism: The natural light-dark cycle regulates melatonin production, which in turn influences sleep and wakefulness.
findings.quote: diurnal and nocturnal fluctuations in melatonin modulates sleep and wakefulness

findings.antecedent: Morning (light exposure)
findings.mechanism: Morning light exposure stimulates cortisol release, preparing the body for daily activity.
findings.quote: elevated cortisol levels in the morning prime the body for activity

findings.antecedent: Night (darkness)
findings.mechanism: Lower cortisol levels at night promote relaxation and prepare the body for sleep.
findings.quote: lower cortisol levels at night encourage relaxation.

findings.antecedent: Slowly changing light
findings.mechanism: Special photoreceptive ganglion cells in the retina regulate neural hormone systems to synchronize bodily responses with the time of day.
findings.quote: slowly changing light regulates a complex system of neural hormone responses to synchronize psycho-physiological responses with the time of day [23, 24].

findings.antecedent: Cones (retinal photoreceptors)
findings.mechanism: Beyond vision, cones contribute to the regulation of non-visual physiological processes like circadian rhythms.
findings.quote: the cones, previously thought to function solely as vision receptors, also play a role in eliciting such non-visual responses, in certain conditions [25].

findings.antecedent: Brief exposure (less than 15m) to red, bright white, and dark light conditions (during memory task)
findings.mechanism: Different light spectra influence autonomic nervous system activity and stress responses during cognitive tasks.
findings.quote: heart rate variability... was highly significantly different during memory task performance during brief exposure (less than 15 m) to red, bright white, and dark conditions.

findings.antecedent: Red light (during rest)
findings.mechanism: Red light promotes physiological relaxation, as indicated by appropriate HRV changes.
findings.quote: red light regulated cardiac responses, with appropriate HRV relaxation during rest

findings.antecedent: Red light (during memory task)
findings.mechanism: Red light supports physiological activation necessary for cognitive performance during a memory task.
findings.quote: and activation during the memory task.

findings.antecedent: Bright white light with a blue peak
findings.mechanism: Blue-rich light promotes sustained physiological arousal, leading to constant heart rate activation.
findings.quote: bright white light with a blue peak was associated with constant heart rate activation throughout the experiment [28].

findings.antecedent: Red light vs. bright white light conditions
findings.mechanism: Different light spectra elicit distinct patterns of electrical activity in the brain.
findings.quote: brainwaves recorded via a 256 electrode EEG array tended to be different during red versus bright white light conditions in a single subject self-control study [29].

findings.antecedent: Green light
findings.mechanism: Green light, under specific conditions, can influence the body's internal biological clock.
findings.quote: green light also stimulates circadian responses under certain conditions [30].

findings.antecedent: "Full spectrum" electrical lighting (limited spectral peaks)
findings.mechanism: Lack of conclusive evidence regarding the specific effects of this type of lighting on human physiology and behavior.
findings.quote: the influence of “full spectrum” electrical lighting, which has a limited number of spectral peaks within the range of visible light, has yet to be established [31].

findings.antecedent: Abnormal pattern of light-dark exposure (night-shift work)
findings.mechanism: Disruption of natural circadian rhythms due to altered light exposure patterns may contribute to increased cancer risk.
findings.quote: cancer rates in night-shift workers... may be related to an abnormal pattern of light-dark exposure [32, 33].

findings.antecedent: Low levels of lighting during the day
findings.consequent: Mental health status (including seasonal affective disorder)
findings.mechanism: Insufficient daytime light exposure negatively impacts mood regulation and overall mental well-being.
findings.quote: Low levels of lighting during the day have been associated with mental health status, including seasonal affective disorder

findings.antecedent: Low levels of lighting during the day
findings.consequent: Recovery times for mental health patients
findings.mechanism: Inadequate light exposure can hinder the healing and recovery processes in mental health patients.
findings.quote: and longer recovery times for mental health patients [34].

findings.antecedent: Inadequate lighting
findings.mechanism: Poor lighting conditions can impair cognitive processes such as attention and information processing.
findings.quote: Diminished cognitive function has also been associated with inadequate lighting

findings.antecedent: Seasonal reduction in light
findings.mechanism: Seasonal changes in light may affect cognitive performance and vigilance, leading to an increase in medication errors.
findings.quote: pharmaceutical medication error rates have been correlated with seasonal reduction in light [35].

stimuli.description: Immersive 3D virtual reality CAVE displaying full-scale building models, hospital rooms, nurses' stations, and spaces with/without wayfinding cues.
SoniCAVEM virtual sound simulation environment merging ultrahigh definition recordings and sound simulations of real environments with visualizations.

limitations: An approach that gives credit to the proportion of space with daylight, rather than crediting adjustable lighting systems that provide for individual needs, is unlikely to address the range of human conditions, and the dynamically changing nature of functions that take place in architectural settings.
